claim: Chromosome alignment in the middle of the bipolar spindle is a hallmark of metazoan cell divisions.
source: Chromosome alignment in the middle of the bipolar spindle is a hallmark of metazoan cell divisions.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about metazoan cell divisions.

claim: When the metaphase plate position is offset by creating an asymmetric centriole distribution on each pole, metaphase plates relocate to the middle of the spindle before anaphase.
source: When we offset the metaphase plate position by creating an asymmetric centriole distribution on each pole, we find that metaphase plates relocate to the middle of the spindle before anaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations presented in the manuscript, including tracking data and imaging.

claim: The spindle assembly checkpoint enables the metaphase plate centering mechanism by providing cells enough time to correct metaphase plate position.
source: The spindle assembly checkpoint enables this centering mechanism by providing cells enough time to correct metaphase plate position.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing timing differences and SAC inhibition experiments.

claim: The checkpoint responds to unstable kinetochore–microtubule attachments resulting from an imbalance in microtubule stability between the two half-spindles in cells with an asymmetric centriole distribution.
source: The checkpoint responds to unstable kinetochore–microtubule attachments resulting from an imbalance in microtubule stability between the two half-spindles in cells with an asymmetric centriole distribution.
evidence: This is supported by cold-stable assays, SKAP staining, and other experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Inactivation of the checkpoint prior to metaphase plate centering leads to asymmetric cell divisions and daughter cells of unequal size.
source: Inactivation of the checkpoint prior to metaphase plate centering leads to asymmetric cell divisions and daughter cells of unequal size
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Mps1 inhibition and KIF2a/MCAK depletion experiments.

claim: If the checkpoint is inactivated after the metaphase plate has centered its position, symmetric cell divisions ensue.
source: in contrast, if the checkpoint is inactivated after the metaphase plate has centered its position, symmetric cell divisions ensue.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from timing-specific Mps1 inhibition experiments.

claim: The equatorial position of the metaphase plate is essential for symmetric cell divisions.
source: This indicates that the equatorial position of the metaphase plate is essential for symmetric cell divisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing asymmetric divisions when plate position is not centered.

claim: A centered metaphase plate is established even in asymmetrically dividing cells.
source: A centered metaphase plate is established even in asymmetrically dividing cells, where daughter cells of unequal size are obtained by an asymmetric positioning of the spindle prior to anaphase (e.g., in Caenorhabditis elegans embryos) or an asymmetric elongation of the spindle in anaphase (e.g., in Drosophila melanogaster embryonic neuroblasts [Kaltschmidt et al., 2000; Schneider and Bowerman, 2003]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The reason why the metaphase plate is located in the middle of the spindle is not known.
source: However, the reason why the metaphase plate is located in the middle of the spindle is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: One hypothesis is that the centered position facilitates the synchronous arrival of chromosomes at spindle poles during anaphase to prevent chromosomes from being caught on the wrong side of the cytokinetic furrow.
source: One hypothesis is that the centered position facilitates the synchronous arrival of chromosomes at spindle poles during anaphase to prevent chromosomes from being caught on the wrong side of the cytokinetic furrow (Nicklas and Arana, 1992; Goshima and Scholey, 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The equatorial positioning of the metaphase plate is not a mere consequence of bipolar kinetochore–microtubule attachments.
source: Elegant work in meiotic praying mantis cells demonstrated that the equatorial positioning of the metaphase plate is not a mere consequence of bipolar kinetochore–microtubule attachments, as trivalent sex-chromosome align in the middle of the spindle, even though trivalent attachment does not favor an equatorial position (Nicklas and Arana, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An asymmetry in centriole numbers at spindle poles led to an asymmetric metaphase plate position in Chlamydomonas rheinhardtii and C. elegans.
source: Moreover, previous studies in Chlamydomonas rheinhardtii and C. elegans showed that an asymmetry in centriole numbers at spindle poles led to an asymmetric metaphase plate position, even though chromosomes established bipolar attachments (Greenan et al., 2010; Keller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In algae, longer half-spindles were associated with the pole containing fewer centrioles.
source: While in algae, longer half-spindles were associated with the pole containing fewer centrioles, in nematodes, longer half-spindles emanated from the pole containing more centrioles.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in the literature.

claim: In nematodes, longer half-spindles emanated from the pole containing more centrioles.
source: While in algae, longer half-spindles were associated with the pole containing fewer centrioles, in nematodes, longer half-spindles emanated from the pole containing more centrioles.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in the literature.

claim: Wild-type HeLa cells have a broad distribution of half-spindle ratios during metaphase centered around median R = 0.98.
source: By plotting the ratio R of the half-spindle lengths of metaphase cells at the onset of our recordings (first three time points), we found a broad distribution centered around median R = 0.98, which represents nearly equal half-spindle lengths.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements and tracking data.

claim: Cells entering anaphase have a sharp distribution of half-spindle ratios with median R = 1.02.
source: When analyzing the subset of cells that entered anaphase during our recordings 30 s before anaphase, we found a sharp R distribution in the middle of the spindle (median R = 1.02; Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Less than 10% of cells at anaphase onset have R values smaller than 0.85 or larger than 1.15.
source: less than 10% of the R values were smaller than 0.85 or larger than 1.15 at anaphase onset, while in the metaphase population over 24.2% were outside of these boundaries.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: In the metaphase population, over 24.2% of R values are outside the boundaries of 0.85 to 1.15.
source: less than 10% of the R values were smaller than 0.85 or larger than 1.15 at anaphase onset, while in the metaphase population over 24.2% were outside of these boundaries.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Sas-6 is a protein required for centriole duplication.
source: To test this hypothesis, we aimed to create asymmetric spindles by generating cells with an asymmetric centriole distribution, using small interfering (si)RNAs against Sas-6, a protein required for centriole duplication (Leidel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Every wild-type mitotic cell contains four centrioles: one oldest (grandmother) centriole, one older (mother) centriole, and their two respective daughter centrioles.
source: Every wild-type mitotic cell contains four centrioles: one oldest (grandmother) centriole, one older (mother) centriole, and their two respective daughter centrioles (Nigg and Raff, 2009), which all have different eGFP-centrin signal intensities (Kuo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A 24-hr Sas-6 depletion led to a mix of cells with two centrioles per pole, one centriole per pole, or one pole with one centriole and the other pole with two centrioles.
source: A 24-hr Sas-6 depletion led to a mix of cells with two centrioles per pole, one centriole per pole, or one pole with one centriole and the other pole with two centrioles (called from here on 2:2, 1:1, or 2:1 cells; Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: In 2:1 cells, it was most often the oldest centriole that gave rise to a daughter centriole.
source: Our intensity measurements revealed that in 2:1 cells it was most often the oldest centriole that gave rise to a daughter centriole, probably due to limiting levels of Sas-6 (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on intensity measurements performed by the authors.

claim: The distribution of half-spindle ratios during metaphase was broad in 2:2 or 1:1 cells, but on average the plate was located in the middle of the cell.
source: Tracking of HeLa eGFP-centrin1/CENPA cells indicated that the distribution of half-spindle ratios during metaphase was broad in 2:2 or 1:1 cells, but that on average the plate was located in the middle of the cell (median R = 1.04 (2:2) and 1.03 (1:1)
evidence: This is supported by tracking data from the experiments.

claim: In 2:1 cells, there are two half-spindles of unequal length, with a shorter half-spindle associated with the pole containing one centriole (median R = 1.12).
source: In 2:1 cells, we found two half-spindles of unequal length, with a shorter half-spindle associated with the pole containing one centriole (median R = 1.12, p < 0.0001 in Mann–Whitney U test compared to symmetric distribution; R > 1.15 in 42.9% of the cells; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The asymmetry in 2:1 cells was corrected before anaphase onset (median R = 1.03).
source: This asymmetry was corrected before anaphase onset (median R = 1.03; Figure 1F), consistent with the existence of a centering process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cells center the plate position over time while reducing the variability in metaphase plate position.
source: By plotting R over time in 15 cells that spend at least 7 min in metaphase before entering anaphase, we could directly observe how cells centered the plate position over time, while reducing the variability in metaphase plate position (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: A 2:2, 1:1, or a 2:1 centriole configuration affected neither the timing of bipolar spindle assembly nor the time it took to align all chromosomes on the metaphase plate.
source: A 2:2, 1:1, or a 2:1 centriole configuration affected neither the timing of bipolar spindle assembly nor the time it took to align all chromosomes on the metaphase plate (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by timing measurements shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Anaphase onset was delayed by 12 min in 2:1 cells when compared to 2:2 or wild-type cells.
source: Anaphase onset, however, was delayed by 12 min (Figure 2C, p = 0.003 in Mann–Whitney U test) in 2:1 cells, when compared to 2:2 or wild-type cells
evidence: This is supported by timing measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 2:1 cells spend twice the amount of time in metaphase compared to control cells.
source: resulting in 2:1 cells spending twice the amount of time in metaphase (Figure 2D, p = 0.015 in Mann–Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by timing measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Anaphase was not delayed in 1:1 cells.
source: In contrast, anaphase was not delayed in 1:1 cells, indicating that the longer metaphase timing seen in 2:1 cells was not caused by the loss of daughter centrioles, but the consequence of centriole asymmetry (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This is supported by timing measurements shown in Figure 2C,E.

claim: The anaphase delay in 2:1 cells depends on the spindle assembly checkpoint.
source: In the absence of Mad2, 2:2, 2:1, 1:1, or control-treated cells had the same anaphase timing, indicating that the anaphase delay in 2:1 cells depends on the SAC (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Mad2 depletion experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Prolonging metaphase in siSas-6-treated cells by 1 hr with MG132 resulted in a symmetric plate position in 2:1 cells (median R = 0.98).
source: To test whether metaphase plate position is corrected as a result of the additional time provided by the SAC, we prolonged metaphase in siSas-6-treated cells by 1 hr by adding the proteasome inhibitor MG132 and found a symmetric plate position in 2:1 cells (median R = 0.98; Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: When the SAC was abrogated in metaphase cells by adding an Mps1 inhibitor, 53% of 2:1 cells entered anaphase with symmetric spindles, while 47% had asymmetric spindles.
source: In contrast, when we abrogated the SAC in metaphase cells by adding an inhibitor of the SAC kinase Mps1, MPS1-IN (Kwiatkowski et al., 2010), 2:1 cells showed a bimodal distribution: 53% entered anaphase with symmetric spindles, with a median R centered around 1, however, the other 47% had asymmetric spindles with a distribution centered around R = 1.15 (Figure 2H, Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.032 when compared to untreated 2:1 cells at anaphase onset).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Loss of 2 daughter centrioles in Sas-6-depleted cells did not reduce the polar ejection force.
source: Loss of 2 daughter centrioles in Sas-6-depleted cells (one in each pole), however, did not reduce this distance, indicating that daughter centriole loss does not reduce the polar ejection force (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by distance measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There were no significant differences for TPX-2 or for phosphorylated Aurora-A between the two spindle poles in Sas-6-depleted 2:1 cells.
source: however, by quantitative immunofluorescence we found no significant differences for TPX-2 or for phosphorylated Aurora-A (the active form of Aurora-A) between the two spindle poles in Sas-6-depleted 2:1 cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Centrobin localizes only to daughter centrioles.
source: Next, we quantified the levels of centrobin, which stabilizes microtubule minus-ends, since it localizes only to daughter centrioles (Zou et al., 2005; Jeffery et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Centrobin was only present on the pole with two centrioles in 2:1 cells.
source: Consistent with the daughter-specific localization, centrobin was only present on the pole with two centrioles in 2:1 cells
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: α-tubulin density in each half-spindle and the abundance of centrosome proteins γ-tubulin, pericentrin, ninein, and p150glued on the two spindle poles in 2:1 cells were as symmetric as in wild-type or 2:2 cells.
source: in contrast, α-tubulin density in each half-spindle and the abundance of the centrosome proteins γ-tubulin, pericentrin, ninein, and p150glued (a marker for the dynein/dynactin motor complex) on the two spindle poles in 2:1 cells were as symmetric as in wild-type or 2:2 cells (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: In 75% of 2:2 or 1:1 cells, the microtubule minus-ends showed the same stability at both spindle poles.
source: The stability of kinetochore–microtubules varied from cell to cell, but in 75% of the 2:2 or 1:1 cells the microtubule minus-ends showed the same stability at both spindle poles (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is supported by cold-stable assay data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: In 2:1 cells, an unequal stability of the minus-ends was visible in over 50% of the cells.
source: In contrast, in 2:1 cells, an unequal stability of the minus-ends was visible in over 50% of the cells, and in most cases it was the pole with 2 centrioles that had more stable minus-ends (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is supported by cold-stable assay data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: In most 2:1 cells with unequal minus-end stability, it was the pole with 2 centrioles that had more stable minus-ends.
source: In contrast, in 2:1 cells, an unequal stability of the minus-ends was visible in over 50% of the cells, and in most cases it was the pole with 2 centrioles that had more stable minus-ends (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is supported by cold-stable assay data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: More than 70% of the spindles in 2:1 eGFP-centrin1/mRFP-α-tubulin cells were rotating.
source: We also noted in our live-cell imaging experiments that >70% of the spindles in 2:1 eGFP-centrin1/mRFP-α-tubulin cells (but not 2:2 or 1:1 cells) were rotating
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging observations.

claim: MG132 treatment leads to symmetric spindles in 2:1 cells and is accompanied by an equalization in microtubule stability at the two spindle poles.
source: To confirm this hypothesis, we first tested whether a 1-hr MG132 treatment, which leads to symmetric spindles in 2:1 cells, is accompanied by an equalization in microtubule stability at the two spindle poles. While in control-treated cells, we saw an unequal stability of the minus-ends in 49 ± 4% of the 2:1 cells, this was only the case in 22 ± 6% of the MG132-treated 2:1 cells (p = 0.0275 in unpaired t-test; Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: KIF2a/MCAK depletion per se did not affect the position of the metaphase plate (median R = 1.01).
source: KIF2a/MCAK depletion per se did not affect the position of the metaphase plate (median R = 1.01) or the ratio of cells with rotating spindles (Figure 3K,L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3K,L.

claim: When KIF2a/MCAK was co-depleted in 2:1 cells, the spindle asymmetry was statistically less pronounced (median spindle ratio R = 1.08).
source: However, when KIF2a/MCAK was co-depleted in 2:1 cells, the spindle asymmetry was statistically less pronounced (median spindle ratio R = 1.08 and 19.2% R > 1.15 compared to median R = 1.12 and 42.9% R > 1.15 in Sas-6 deplete cells, p = 0.039 Mann–Whitney test), and spindles did not rotate (Figure 3L,M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3L,M.

claim: Brief 30 min, 10 nM taxol treatment of Sas-6-depleted 2:1 cells resulted in cells much closer to symmetry (median R = 1.02).
source: To corroborate these results, we also stabilized microtubules by applying a brief, 30 min, 10 nM taxol treatment to Sas-6-depleted cells. While control (DMSO)-treated 2:1 cells were still asymmetric (median R = 1.23 and 56.3% R > 1.15), taxol-treated cells were much closer to symmetry (median R = 1.02 and 13.3% R > 1.15, p = 0.0062; Figure 3N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3N.

claim: Loss of a single centriole leads to a difference in minus-end microtubule stability between the two spindle poles.
source: We conclude that loss of a single centriole leads to a difference in minus-end microtubule stability between the two spindle poles
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including cold-stable assays and drug treatments.

claim: The difference in minus-end microtubule stability plays a large role in the asymmetric positioning of the metaphase plate.
source: that this difference plays a large role in the asymmetric positioning of the metaphase plate
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that stabilizing microtubules reduces spindle asymmetry.

claim: Cells reduce the difference in minus-end stability as they center the metaphase plate before anaphase onset.
source: and that cells reduce this difference as they center the metaphase plate before anaphase onset.
evidence: This is inferred from the MG132 experiments showing equalization of stability over time.

claim: There was no difference in inter-kinetochore distances in 2:1 cells compared to control cells.
source: When we tracked kinetochores in 2:1 eGFP-centrin1/CENPA cells, however, we found no difference in inter-kinetochore distances or the oscillatory sister-kinetochore movements along the spindle axis (Figure 4A,B; Jaqaman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by kinetochore tracking data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: There was no difference in oscillatory sister-kinetochore movements along the spindle axis in 2:1 cells.
source: When we tracked kinetochores in 2:1 eGFP-centrin1/CENPA cells, however, we found no difference in inter-kinetochore distances or the oscillatory sister-kinetochore movements along the spindle axis (Figure 4A,B; Jaqaman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by kinetochore tracking data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The intra-kinetochore distance between CENPA and HEC1 showed no change in 2:1 cells compared to 2:2 or 1:1 cells.
source: we further measured the intra-kinetochore distance between CENPA and the outer kinetochore protein HEC1 and found no change in 2:1 cells compared to 2:2 or 1:1 cells (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by distance measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The observed intra-kinetochore distance of 110 nm is consistent with previous studies.
source: the observed distance of 110 nm is consistent with previous studies (Wan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to a cited previous study.

claim: There was a small but non-significant increase in the proportion of Mad2-positive 2:1 cells compared to control cells.
source: When compared to 2:2, 1:1, or wild-type cells, we found a small but non-significant increase in the proportion of Mad2-positive 2:1 cells (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 22% of 2:1 cells have partially unstable kinetochore–microtubules as indicated by SKAP-negative kinetochores.
source: Such cells were rare in wild-type, 2:2, or 1:1 cells (<10%), but formed a substantial proportion of 2:1 cells (22%; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by SKAP staining data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SKAP-negative kinetochores in 2:1 cells were distributed in a symmetric manner.
source: These SKAP-negative kinetochores were distributed in a symmetric manner (were present both on the 1- or 2-centriole side; data not shown)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Brief treatment with 10 nmol taxol caused all SKAP-negative kinetochores in 2:1 cells to disappear.
source: and they all disappeared if 2:1 cells were briefly treated with 10 nmol taxol (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A 1-hr treatment with MG132 abolished the subpopulation of 2:1 cells with SKAP-negative kinetochores.
source: Moreover a 1-hr treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 also abolished the subpopulation of 2:1 cells with SKAP-negative kinetochores (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In 2:1 cells, sister-kinetochores form amphitelic microtubule attachments, but differences in minus-end stability delay stabilization of kinetochore–microtubule attachments in both half-spindles.
source: Overall this suggested that in 2:1 cells, sister-kinetochores form amphitelic microtubule attachments, but that differences in minus-end stability delay stabilization of kinetochore–microtubule attachments in both half-spindles, as reflected by higher levels of SKAP-negative kinetochores.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Laser-ablation of one daughter centriole in metaphase cells resulted in an asymmetric plate location, with R increasing from 1.06 to 1.16 on average.
source: As in Sas-6-depleted cells, 2:1 cells generated by microsurgery resulted in an asymmetric plate location, as, on average, R increased from 1.06 to 1.16 after laser-ablation (Figure 4G,H and Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by laser-ablation experiments shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: Laser-ablated cells displayed a reduced inter-kinetochore distance (mean of 1.03 μm before ablation to 0.95 μm after ablation).
source: These cells displayed a reduced inter-kinetochore distance (mean of 1.03 μm before ablation to 0.95 μm after the ablation, p = 0.001 in paired two-tailed t-test), which led to a prolonged metaphase arrest (Figure 4I)
evidence: This is supported by measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Loss of a single daughter centriole can directly affect force generation at sister-kinetochores.
source: This confirmed that loss of a single daughter centriole can directly affect force generation at sister-kinetochores
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the laser-ablation experiments.

claim: Acute laser-ablation of a daughter centriole in metaphase has a more severe effect on the forces acting on kinetochores than Sas-6 depletion.
source: We also conclude that an acute laser-ablation of a daughter centriole in metaphase has a more severe effect on the forces acting on kinetochore than Sas-6 depletion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the two experimental approaches.

claim: Aurora-B inhibition does not overcome a SAC-dependent mitotic arrest caused by unattached kinetochores.
source: Aurora-B inhibition does not overcome a SAC-dependent mitotic arrest caused by unattached kinetochores (nocodazole treatment), but overcomes a mitotic arrest caused by insufficient tension at sister-kinetochores in monopolar spindles (monastrol treatment), as Aurora-B inhibition stabilizes kinetochore–microtubules and prevents loss of kinetochore–microtubule attachment (Figure 5A; Ditchfield et al., 2003; Lampson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous work.

claim: Aurora-B inhibition overcomes a mitotic arrest caused by insufficient tension at sister-kinetochores in monopolar spindles.
source: Aurora-B inhibition does not overcome a SAC-dependent mitotic arrest caused by unattached kinetochores (nocodazole treatment), but overcomes a mitotic arrest caused by insufficient tension at sister-kinetochores in monopolar spindles (monastrol treatment), as Aurora-B inhibition stabilizes kinetochore–microtubules and prevents loss of kinetochore–microtubule attachment (Figure 5A; Ditchfield et al., 2003; Lampson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous work.

claim: When Aurora-B was acutely inhibited in metaphase 2:1 cells, cells entered anaphase with asymmetric spindles (median R = 1.18).
source: When we acutely inhibited Aurora-B in metaphase 2:1 cells, cells entered anaphase with asymmetric spindles (median R = 1.18, Mann–Whitney U test, p = 7.57 × 10−6 when compared to anaphase onset without Aurora-B inhibitor), indicating that a stabilization of kinetochore–microtubules satisfies the SAC in 2:1 cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Stabilization of kinetochore–microtubules satisfies the SAC in 2:1 cells.
source: When we acutely inhibited Aurora-B in metaphase 2:1 cells, cells entered anaphase with asymmetric spindles (median R = 1.18, Mann–Whitney U test, p = 7.57 × 10−6 when compared to anaphase onset without Aurora-B inhibitor), indicating that a stabilization of kinetochore–microtubules satisfies the SAC in 2:1 cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from the Aurora-B inhibition experiments.

claim: Depletion of KIF2a/MCAK per se did not affect plate position at anaphase onset (median R = 1.03).
source: Depletion of KIF2a/MCAK per se did not affect plate position at anaphase onset (median R = 1.03); however, it allowed 2:1 cells to enter anaphase with asymmetric spindles (median R 1.08, p < 0.0001 compared to symmetric distribution in Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: KIF2a/MCAK depletion allowed 2:1 cells to enter anaphase with asymmetric spindles (median R 1.08).
source: Depletion of KIF2a/MCAK per se did not affect plate position at anaphase onset (median R = 1.03); however, it allowed 2:1 cells to enter anaphase with asymmetric spindles (median R 1.08, p < 0.0001 compared to symmetric distribution in Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: KIF2a/MCAK depletion rescued the anaphase timing difference in 2:1 cells compared to 2:2 cells.
source: KIF2a/MCAK depletion also rescued the anaphase timing difference in 2:1 cells compared to 2:2 cells and led to the correct loading of SKAP on kinetochores (Figure 5D,E
evidence: This is supported by timing measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: KIF2a/MCAK depletion led to the correct loading of SKAP on kinetochores in 2:1 cells.
source: KIF2a/MCAK depletion also rescued the anaphase timing difference in 2:1 cells compared to 2:2 cells and led to the correct loading of SKAP on kinetochores (Figure 5D,E
evidence: This is supported by SKAP staining data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Co-depletion of KIF2a/MCAK overrides the SAC response in 2:1 cells.
source: This showed that co-depletion of KIF2a/MCAK overrides the SAC response in 2:1 cells, leaving them no time to center the metaphase plate
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Unstable kinetochore–microtubules cause the SAC-dependent anaphase delay in 2:1 cells.
source: indicating that unstable kinetochore–microtubules cause the SAC-dependent anaphase delay.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the KIF2a/MCAK depletion experiments.

claim: KIF2a/MCAK co-depletion did not suppress a mitotic arrest caused by insufficient tension or unattached kinetochores.
source: KIF2a/MCAK co-depletion, however, did not suppress a mitotic arrest caused by the presence of insufficient tension (monastrol treatment) or unattached kinetochores (nocodazole treatment; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: KIF2a/MCAK-depleted 2:1 cells had slightly higher rates of chromosome segregation errors compared to KIF2a/MCAK-depleted cells (statistically insignificant).
source: We found that KIF2a/MCAK/Sas-6-depleted 2:1 cells had slightly higher rates of chromosome segregation errors (statistically insignificant difference, p = 0.4713, Fischer's exact test) when compared to KIF2a/MCAK-depleted cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of segregation errors shown in Figure 6A.

claim: KIF2a/MCAK-depleted 2:1 cells underwent asymmetric cell divisions, yielding two daughter cells of different volumes.
source: Strikingly KIF2a/MCAK-depleted 2:1 cells also underwent asymmetric cell divisions, yielding two daughter cells of different volumes (Figure 6B and Videos 5, 6)
evidence: This is supported by cell volume measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The two daughter cell volumes never differed by more than 20% in wild-type or KIF2a/MCAK depleted cells.
